interop_reason: A traveller or agent cannot safely complete entry unless the origin and destination understand the destination's approval, refusal and validity conditions.
note: Through the Netcode for GameObjects package a server can approve or refuse each arriving client in a callback and attach a reason that the client receives. Missing: a validity limit on the approval, and any approval given before the client arrives; the page also says approval is not supported with the distributed authority topology.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: Choosing and dispatching internal GPU computation does not require agreement between the systems that exchange an asset.
note: The engine supports compute shaders outside the normal rendering pipeline, with graphics API and platform support conditions.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: An asset can still load with fallback materials when its shaders are not understood, but authored appearance degrades.
note: Custom shaders consume HLSL and ShaderLab; pipeline-specific bindings are required and do not imply unchanged cross-engine materials.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: A receiver that cannot evaluate the transmitted curves and surfaces cannot reconstruct an asset whose geometry is carried in that form.
note: The Splines package defines stored curves with a common data model and tools for evaluating and authoring paths.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: Losing an exchanged emitter's parameters removes or changes visual effects while the containing asset or avatar can still arrive.
note: Particle systems simulate authored effect parameters; the captured page does not establish exchange of emitter descriptions to another runtime.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: A stripped provenance record weakens trust in an arriving asset while the asset remains usable.
note: Unity can sign exported asset packages so their origin and integrity can be checked, but nothing recovers a lost provenance record from a content fingerprint or watermark. Searched the Unity 6.6 manual word index (3,667 pages; package manuals not included) for watermark, fingerprint, provenance and C2PA on 2026-10-20; the only hits were package signing, build fingerprints on Android and browser fingerprinting.

subject: Unity
capability: Declarative styling carried apart from the content
interop_reason: Without shared styling rules, a moved scene can still load while its metadata-driven visibility and appearance change.
note: Unity's UI Toolkit applies style sheets in USS, whose selectors pick which user interface elements a rule affects, so styling is kept apart from the structure. Missing: any such styling for three-dimensional scene content selected by content metadata; this covers user interface elements only.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: A default asset can arrive when variant selection is lost, but the chosen configuration of the asset or avatar changes.
note: Prefab variants preserve alternate authored configurations and select them as distinct prefab assets, with variant overrides taking precedence.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: A receiver that cannot decode the exchanged cells and their properties cannot reconstruct content represented as a voxel volume.
note: Unity has 3D textures, a stored volume of values in three dimensions that shaders sample, which covers storing a cell volume. Missing: any exchange form for voxel data, cell properties beyond texture channels, or updates; searched the Unity 6.6 manual word index (3,667 pages; package manuals not included) for voxel on 2026-10-20 and found only collision caching and occlusion-culling pages.

subject: Unity
capability: Hit test against the real world
interop_reason: A disagreement about sensing hit results makes placement and interaction worse, while manual placement can keep the experience usable.
note: AR Foundation ray casts intersect detected physical-environment trackables, with supported hit types determined by the target provider.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: If two systems disagree on what a contained experience may do, the containment either fails or becomes a security hole; there is no partial agreement that works.
note: Unity's additive scene loading (LoadSceneMode.Additive) loads another scene with its own GameObjects, MonoBehaviours and physics into the current world. Each loaded scene runs its own scripts within the shared update loop. But Unity defines no formal containment boundary — no event propagation protocol between host and contained scenes, no consumption rule, and no stated boundary for third-party experience isolation.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: A coupling that carries change without anyone crossing needs both ends to agree on authority, ordering and settlement, or the two worlds silently diverge.
note: Unity's networking (Netcode for GameObjects, Netcode for Entities) replicates state within a single game session. Cross-world state coupling — where one Unity world mutates another's state with nobody in either — is not a built-in capability. Developers can build it with application code, but the engine defines no such mechanism.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: The agent use case says an agent pays for what it uses; if payer and payee share no payment exchange, the payment cannot happen at all.
note: The optional Unity In-App Purchasing package gives one API over Apple App Store, Google Play and Direct-to-Consumer payment providers, and each store or provider handles the purchase flow and payment processing. It is a person-facing store checkout; it defines no payment protocol of its own and no agent payment.

subject: Unity
capability: Entitlements and licence checks at use
interop_reason: A destination that cannot read a grant must refuse the item, the entry or the agent, or admit it blindly.
note: Through the Unity In-App Purchasing package 5.0, a game calls CheckEntitlement on a product and receives an entitlement status such as fully entitled or not entitled. The store backend supplies the holder binding; the package page defines no transfer rules or recognition across stores. The editor LicensingUtility and private content bucket tokens are separate checks, shown as context.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: A grant can still be checked with its issuer without a portable receipt, but a third system cannot verify the purchase on its own.
note: Through the Unity In-App Purchasing package the engine validates store-issued receipts by signature and application identifier and exposes the product, date and transaction identifier. Missing: Unity defines no receipt of its own, only Google Play and Apple receipts validate, and nothing binds recipient and resource in a store-independent way another system could check.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: Credentials still verify without a shared registry, but each receiver must decide alone whom to trust, so acceptance differs from world to world.
note: Unity is a real-time engine and editor, and the identity provider list in its Authentication package configures player sign-in for one project rather than a shared governed registry of accepted issuers.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: Assets can still move one at a time, but a place that cannot leave its host as a whole has to be rebuilt by hand when the host changes or closes.
note: Scenes and prefabs can be saved in a documented text format (UnityYAML), and parts of a project move between projects as .unitypackage archives that keep folder structure and import settings. There is no whole-place export in an open interchange format and no statement of what survives outside Unity; the package format is Unity's own.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: The object model arrives from another system, so its format and units must be readable by the tracker, while the tracking itself stays on the device.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: A digital twin can still be shown without a shared binding, but each data source must be wired by hand; the Atlas's four use cases do not yet include digital twins, so the row is recorded against content that moves.

Treated as partial, with the missing part being a documented, built-in source binding.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: Training still finishes without a portable record, but the result stays in one vendor's dashboard instead of travelling with the person.

Searched unity.com/solutions/immersive-training, unity.com/resources/pinnacle-solutions, the docs.unity.com Analytics overview, and web searches limited to unity.com, docs.unity3d.com and docs.unity.com for xAPI, SCORM, cmi5, learning record store and learning management system on 2026-10-20; found no Unity-supplied learning-record output. The Unity Manual was not searched in full.

subject: Unity
interop_reason: Sensors and experiences come from different vendors; without a shared signal description each adaptation is wired to one device, though the experience still runs without it.
note: Searched Unity Input System 1.14 (Sensor support, Devices pages) and the Unity OpenXR Plugin 1.15 manual (index, Input pages) for heart, biometric and physiolog on 2026-10-20; no match, and a web search restricted to docs.unity3d.com and unity.com found no first-party body-signal document. The Input System sensor list covers motion, environment and a step counter, but no heart-rate or skin-conductance device. The full Unity manual was not searched.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: How a system turns geometry into pixels never leaves that system, so two runtimes can draw the same scene by different means and nothing crosses.
note: The engine ships deferred and forward rendering paths for desktop and for head-mounted displays, plus a separate mobile path; the pass structure and render graph are engine-internal and are not published as anything a second implementation could follow.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: The graphics interface a runtime targets is a build choice inside one system, and an arriving asset cannot tell the difference.
note: Targets Direct3D 12 and 11, Vulkan and Metal, with the newest features gated on Direct3D 12 and shader model 6; no browser graphics interface is listed as a target, so web reach is by streaming pixels rather than by running the renderer in the client.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: An asset that arrives against a different surface model still loads, but the further apart the two models are the more the look drifts.
note: Surface appearance is authored as a node graph compiled into engine shaders, with the newer layered material system still shipping experimental parts in 5.8; nothing outside the engine evaluates these graphs, so the model is engine-only.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A moved scene whose lights are read differently is lit wrong rather than lost.
note: Lumen is the default dynamic global illumination and reflections system, with hardware and software ray tracing paths, joined in 5.8 by a production-ready many-light system and a cheaper medium-quality global illumination setting; all of it is an engine-private algorithm that no other runtime implements.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Effects applied after the main pass are the receiving system's taste and carry nothing across.
note: A volume placed in the level drives the full post chain, from exposure and colour grading to motion blur and path tracing; the settings are engine assets and do not travel to any other renderer.

subject: Unreal Engine
capability: Level of detail and streaming order
interop_reason: Without an agreed order for what to send first, a large scene still arrives, it just pops and stalls on the way in.
note: The virtualized geometry system streams only the detail that is visible, and world partition adds level-of-detail across a whole map; because the streamed data is the engine's own internal mesh format, another runtime cannot consume the same stream.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Only content captured as splats is affected: a system that cannot draw them shows nothing of it, while mesh content is untouched.
note: Searched the Unreal Engine 5.8 Experimental Features page and the Unreal Engine 5.8 Release Notes for 'splat', 'Gaussian', 'radiance field' and 'NeRF' on 2026-10-19; no Gaussian-splat or radiance-field rendering feature is listed (the only hits were an unrelated depth-of-field splat size and Lumen's irradiance fields). The rest of the 5.8 documentation and the marketplace plugins from other vendors were not searched, so absence from the engine proper is unconfirmed.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: The same holds for point clouds and volumetric video, which travel in forms few systems read.
note: Point clouds come from the LiDAR Point Cloud plugin, which reads the open interchange formats for scanned data; volumetric rendering through heterogeneous volumes and sparse volume textures ships as an experimental engine feature.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Labels, signs and name tags lose their font and layout when the two systems disagree, so the text degrades while the rest of the asset is fine.
note: Solid three-dimensional lettering comes from the Text 3D plugin, which builds geometry from a font; flat interface text uses the engine's own widget system. Neither is a portable text layout model.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Authored viewpoints are part of a scene, and losing them costs the arrival shot, not the scene.
note: Cameras are components and actors with view targets and modifiers; a newer gameplay camera system ships in 5.8 but is still marked experimental, so the camera model is in flux.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: If the receiving system cannot rebuild the same tree, parenting and transforms collapse and the asset does not assemble at all.
note: The world is a set of actors holding attached components; this hierarchy is defined only by the engine's own object system and does not exist outside it.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: The engine is left-handed with the up axis pointing along Z and forward along X, which is the opposite handedness and a different up axis from both glTF and the usual scene description convention, so every import and export has to convert axes and winding.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: The engine's own containers carry nothing outward: authoring uses engine asset and map files, and shipping uses cooked containers holding package, bulk and shader data, both tied to the exact engine build. The real transfer route is the import and export framework, which is file-format agnostic, can run at runtime, and reads and writes the open Khronos transfer format; that route is open to any implementation, but it carries far less than the engine's own files do.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A mesh encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a mesh, and the compression choice is where this usually breaks.
note: Meshes are stored in the engine's own compressed form, and the virtualized geometry path is explicitly described by Epic as an internal mesh format, which is the clearest single statement of geometry lock-in in the documentation.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Device-specific texture compression is the common failure: the model arrives untextured and someone must re-export it.
note: Source images are converted at cook time to the format each target platform wants, with an optional virtual texture path; the choice of format is a project setting, not something carried in an interchange file.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Carrying materials without loss is what "renders in another system" means, and only two subjects reach this row natively today.
note: The glTF exporter can either match simple material patterns or bake complex ones to textures, and it emits a named set of Khronos extensions plus one Epic vendor extension; Epic states plainly that the target format cannot hold everything the engine can express, so material exchange is lossy in the outward direction.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A clip that cannot be read leaves the object still, and an avatar that cannot move is not an avatar.
note: Animation clips are engine assets driven by animation blueprints and a sequencer; clips can be brought in through the import framework but the runtime representation is engine-only.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: The bone hierarchy is what makes a body move correctly elsewhere; without an agreed one, motion has nothing to bind to.
note: Bone hierarchy and binding live in a dedicated skeleton asset that every animation is tied to; the engine defines this itself and does not implement an agreed cross-vendor bone naming scheme.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Blend shapes carry facial detail, so losing them freezes a face rather than stopping the transfer.
note: Shape deformation targets exist inside the engine, but they do not survive export: Epic lists morph target animations among the things the glTF exporter does not carry.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A scene without agreed instancing still loads, it just costs far more memory and frames.
note: Repeated objects use instanced and hierarchical instanced mesh components, and the virtualized geometry path instances as well; the mechanism is engine-internal and has no interchange representation here.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Layered references are a working convenience, and flattening on export is the fallback that keeps the asset moving.
note: Inside the engine, level instances and world partition data layers layer a map from several files. Genuine referencing and override across tools comes from the scene description plugin, which works on the stage directly rather than converting it, and which supports payloads, variants and writing edits back. Epic has taken a public position on the format by joining the Alliance for OpenUSD as a general member, so this is a deliberate bet on an outside standard rather than an engine-only feature; the caveat is that Epic still marks the support beta, and beta support for the composition layer that most interoperability work depends on is a real risk for anyone planning around it.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A metre read as a centimetre makes the asset useless on arrival, and rescaling by hand is the fix the use case forbids.
note: Distance defaults to centimetres, so one engine unit is one centimetre; imports from tools that work in metres need a scale factor, and getting it wrong is the most common cause of wrong-sized content.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: An item that arrives with no readable terms cannot be lawfully worn, shown or sold, so the move fails at the rights boundary even when every byte arrives.
note: Any asset can carry free-form key and value metadata, which could record a creator or intended usage, but the engine defines no licence key and the metadata cannot be read by gameplay code at run time. Nothing states what a recipient may do with the asset in a form a tool can act on.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A signed record of who made an asset lets a receiver trust it; without one the asset still works but nobody can check its history.
note: Searched the Unreal Engine 5.8 documentation pages reachable from its index (157 pages read, not the whole documentation set), the glTF exporter page and web search of dev.epicgames.com for provenance, C2PA, content credentials, signed authorship, asset signing on 2026-10-20; found no signed record of who made an asset. Metadata can hold an unsigned creator name, and packaged files can be signed only to detect tampering, which names no author.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: The portable description of the body is the artefact this use case moves; with no agreement the person arrives as nothing.
note: MetaHuman is Epic's own framework for rigged photorealistic characters and ships as engine plugins; it is a first-party pipeline rather than a portable avatar container, and no engine-neutral avatar format is implemented.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Agreed bone names are what let animation authored anywhere play on the arriving body.
note: The engine has a strong internal convention through its skeleton assets and an abstraction layer (the rig) for mapping between skeletons, but there is no agreed bone naming standard, so transfer between worlds still needs a per-pair mapping.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: The use case names expressions, and named shapes the destination does not know leave a blank face.
note: MetaHuman supplies a named facial control rig and animation can be generated from captured performance. Epic publishes the list of control curves as the MetaHuman Facial Description Standard, which its page defines as the stored representation of MetaHuman facial animation; it does not present the curves as a cross-engine expression or viseme vocabulary, so what survives a move to another world is not stated.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Retargeting is the repair when skeletons differ, so its absence costs motion quality rather than the visit.
note: Animation made for one body can be replayed on another, both between characters sharing a skeleton and, through the rig mapping assets, between skeletons with different bone counts and names; this works only inside the engine.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Equipped items are named in the use case, and attachment points that do not survive leave items on the floor or on the wrong bone.
note: Sockets and component attachment let items be worn or carried, but attachment points are named inside engine assets and carry no meaning outside them.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Reduced forms matter for crowds and weak devices, and their absence costs frames, not presence.
note: Skinned meshes carry reduced LOD variants that the engine can generate, for distance and for weaker devices.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Without a way to bind an avatar to a verifiable identity, the person who arrives cannot be shown to be the person who left.
note: Nothing in the engine ties an avatar to a verifiable credential. The online plugins issue an opaque per-service account identifier at login and nothing beyond it; that asserts an account signed in, not who the holder is, and it carries no meaning to a party outside that service.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Mass and velocity carried across make a moved object behave nearly the same; their absence changes the behaviour without stopping it.
note: Chaos is the built-in physics solution and covers rigid body dynamics directly; it is engine code with no separate specification, though the same job is done by several independent physics libraries elsewhere.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Collision shapes travel separately from visible geometry, and losing them means objects pass through each other until the destination builds its own.
note: Contact shapes are authored separately from visible geometry, with simple and complex collision and a channel and response matrix; the presets are engine configuration and do not travel with an exported model.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Hinges and sliders that do not survive turn an assembly into loose parts, which is a loss of behaviour rather than of the asset.
note: Constraint components and actors provide hinges, sliders and the rest, and physics assets wire them into character rigs.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Friction and restitution numbers mean different things to different solvers, so agreeing on them buys little and each world may keep its own feel.
note: Friction, restitution, density and surface type are set on physical material assets referenced by rendering materials; the values are engine assets and are not carried by any interchange format used here.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Two engines producing the same trajectory would let one object be simulated in two places at once, and nothing does that today.
note: Epic does not claim that the same inputs give the same outcome on different machines; instead the networked physics design assumes divergence and corrects it, with a resimulation mode that replays cached inputs on the client, and that machinery has to be written by hand in C++. Asynchronous stepping is described as improving determinism, not guaranteeing it.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Cloth and hair are the visible part, so a moved avatar arrives stiff rather than absent.
note: Cloth, hair and soft tissue simulation all ship as part of the built-in physics system, including a machine-learning cloth path.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Regions that fire events are part of how content behaves, and their loss makes the content inert rather than unreadable.
note: Trigger actors and overlap events fire when something enters a region; this is a standard engine actor and the pattern is easily reproduced elsewhere.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Positioned sounds are authored into a scene, and losing them leaves a silent room.
note: Sounds are placed in the world and fall off with distance through attenuation shapes; sound generation itself is a signal-processing graph asset with sample-accurate timing.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: How direction is turned into sound at the ears is the receiving system's method, like a rendering method.
note: The engine itself gives you panning and a soundfield submix path for ambisonics, but it ships no binaural head-related transfer renderer of its own: Epic's documentation points at third-party plugins for that. The plugin interface is open C++, so other vendors can and do implement it, which makes this one of the less locked-in parts of the engine.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A space's acoustic description is authored with it, and without agreement the room sounds wrong rather than silent.
note: Rooms colour sound through submix reverb effects and volumes, with the amount of reverb sent scaling with distance from the listener; the settings are engine assets rather than a described acoustic model.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: The receiving runtime works this out from its own geometry, frame by frame.
note: A built-in occlusion pass traces against scene geometry to cut volume and high frequencies when something blocks the path; the trace is cheap and asynchronous, and the approach is generic enough that anything could implement it.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A visitor can be given audio by other means, so disagreement costs quality and scale.

Streaming sound data from the local package into a cache is not network delivery and is not counted.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: A visitor who cannot be heard is diminished but still present, and text remains a fallback.
note: Live voice between players comes from the online services plugins rather than the core engine, so it depends on the operator's chosen service; the engine exposes a voice interface that a different back end could implement.

note: This is the deepest lock-in in the whole subject. subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Disagreement about who owns an arriving object shows up as rubber-banding and contested edits rather than as a failed arrival.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Without agreement the destination sends everything or too little, which costs scale.
note: Both the older replication graph and the newer replication system filter and prioritise per connection so each client gets only what it needs; the newer system is still marked experimental in 5.8 and the older one remains the default.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Latency hiding is local repair work, so its absence is felt as lag.

subject: Unreal Engine
interop_reason: Live audio and video degrade or drop out while the visit continues.

interop_reason: Joining a running world, authentication included, is the door: no agreement, no entry.

subject: Unreal Engine

subject: Unreal Engine

interop_reason: Relationships and standing that do not travel leave the person present but unknown.

Meshes go back out through the world export, which now writes several coordinate channels and keeps mesh names, so this one is genuinely two-way, but what comes back has already lost its pivots and its tree.

The heuristic is what makes rigs built for other platforms work, so in practice it interoperates well, but nothing is guaranteed and there is no declared bone standard to conform to. Digitigrade legs are not supported.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The use case names expressions, and named shapes the destination does not know leave a blank face.
note: Two halves, and they point opposite ways. Visemes ARE an external set: Resonite's Viseme enum is index-for-index the Oculus/OVR LipSync fifteen, proven by Yellow Dog Man's own OVRCompat source. Facial EXPRESSIONS are not: Resonite ships roughly ninety proprietary AvatarExpression names and deliberately does not adopt ARKit or VRCFT Unified Expressions. Adding Unified Expressions to the matching heuristics is an open, unimplemented issue in Resonite's own tracker, and users currently bridge the gap with a third-party mod. Blendshape auto-assignment does opportunistically match VRChat's `vrc.` prefix and some Japanese kana.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Retargeting is the repair when skeletons differ, so its absence costs motion quality rather than the visit.
note: Resonite has no humanoid animation retargeting. Its animation format binds tracks to a node name and a field name, not to a body-part abstraction, so an animation authored for one body does not transfer to another. The documentation goes further and says you cannot drive a VRIK rig with an animation at all — the engine fights it — and recommends posing users with anchors instead.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Equipped items are named in the use case, and attachment points that do not survive leave items on the floor or on the wrong bone.
note: The engine gives you attachment machinery — AvatarObjectSlot and AvatarPoseNode let separate avatar pieces bind to named body nodes, and Snapper handles accessories such as hats and glasses — so items genuinely do travel with a user between worlds inside their inventory. What is missing is an agreed convention for fitting a garment to an unfamiliar body. The wiki's "Avatar standard" page is explicitly a user proposal, with at least one widely used competing fork, and it admits blendshape names are avatar-specific.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Reduced forms matter for crowds and weak devices, and their absence costs frames, not presence.
note: There is no avatar level of detail, no avatar performance ranking, and no built-in avatar culling. Crowd handling is left entirely to user-built systems, and the documentation says plainly that none of them work properly. Resonite's own comparison table for incoming VRChat users lists avatar performance blocking as not applicable.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Without a way to bind an avatar to a verifiable identity, the person who arrives cannot be shown to be the person who left.
note: An avatar can be bound to one cloud user for permission purposes — SimpleAvatarProtection names a single user who may wear, save or export it — but that is asset ownership, not identity. Resonite's docs explicitly warn that what an avatar displays about who you are is not trustworthy: nameplates and badges are avatar-author-controlled and can be faked, and users are told to check the server-side Session screen instead. There is no credential or attestation concept.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Mass and velocity carried across make a moved object behave nearly the same; their absence changes the behaviour without stopping it.
note: The engine ships BepuPhysics2, but rigid bodies are NOT exposed to creators. Resonite's own wiki page for the physics library carries a note on its demonstration video reading that this is what the engine can do, not what is available in Resonite, and points at an open GitHub issue as the tracker for exposing it. What creators actually have is a character controller and collision events. Full rigid-body physics is a named future feature.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Collision shapes travel separately from visible geometry, and losing them means objects pass through each other until the destination builds its own.
note: Eight collider shapes are exposed as components — box, capsule, cone, convex hull, cylinder, mesh, sphere and triangle — each with an offset, a type, a mass and a flag for whether avatars are blocked by it. Collision shapes are authored separately from visible geometry, which is what the capability asks for. There are documented behavioural gaps: active colliders do not raise events against other active colliders, and mesh colliders only collide with primitive colliders.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Hinges and sliders that do not survive turn an assembly into loose parts, which is a loss of behaviour rather than of the asset.
note: Partial: the Joint component rotates a slot about a point or an axis and the Slider component moves one along an axis, both driven by a grabbing user (doors, helmet tops, dials), so hinge-like and slider-like constraints exist for grabbable objects. Missing: no physics-simulated joints, springs or constraints between dynamic bodies are exposed to users. The engine's physics library supports them internally, and the wiki says full rigid-body integration is future work; in the project's 2024-12-15 podcast its developer says springs and joints cannot be done. subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Friction and restitution numbers mean different things to different solvers, so agreeing on them buys little and each world may keep its own feel.
