subject: SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC)
interop_reason: Recorded descriptively by the owner's decision of 2026-09-18: the Atlas records which systems render remotely and does not define an agreement between client and renderer.
note: STAC describes data files for other software to draw and does not render anything, so remote (split) rendering is outside its purpose.

subject: SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC)
interop_reason: A digital twin can still be shown without a shared binding, but each data source must be wired by hand; the Atlas's four use cases do not yet include digital twins, so the row is recorded against content that moves.
note: STAC describes data files and a search interface over them, not live multi-user sessions, so live data binding is outside its purpose.

subject: SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC)
interop_reason: Training still finishes without a portable record, but the result stays in one vendor's dashboard instead of travelling with the person.
note: STAC describes data files and does not store user or world state, so activity and learning records is outside its purpose.

subject: SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC)
interop_reason: Sensors and experiences come from different vendors; without a shared signal description each adaptation is wired to one device, though the experience still runs without it.
note: STAC describes stored data files and has no user input devices, so physiological signals as input is outside its purpose.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: How a system turns geometry into pixels never leaves that system, so two runtimes can draw the same scene by different means and nothing crosses.
note: It draws nothing. It is a document format, an evaluation contract and a set of checkers; the specification's whole output is a verdict and a receipt.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The graphics interface a runtime targets is a build choice inside one system, and an arriving asset cannot tell the difference.
note: It draws nothing, so it targets no graphics interface.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: An asset that arrives against a different surface model still loads, but the further apart the two models are the more the look drifts.
note: It describes no surface appearance and evaluates nothing at render time.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A moved scene whose lights are read differently is lit wrong rather than lost.
note: It draws nothing, so it has no light, shadow or global illumination model.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Effects applied after the main pass are the receiving system's taste and carry nothing across.
note: It draws nothing, so there is no render pass to follow.

subject: Universal Manifest
capability: Level of detail and streaming order
interop_reason: Without an agreed order for what to send first, a large scene still arrives, it just pops and stalls on the way in.
note: It streams no geometry, so it has no detail levels or send order to choose.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Only content captured as splats is affected: a system that cannot draw them shows nothing of it, while mesh content is untouched.
note: It renders nothing and defines no splat or radiance-field data.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The same holds for point clouds and volumetric video, which travel in forms few systems read.
note: It renders nothing and defines no point cloud or voxel data.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Labels, signs and name tags lose their font and layout when the two systems disagree, so the text degrades while the rest of the asset is fine.
note: It renders nothing, so it has no fonts or text layout.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Authored viewpoints are part of a scene, and losing them costs the arrival shot, not the scene.
note: It defines no viewpoints; its only camera mention is a sensor class named in consent keys.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: If the receiving system cannot rebuild the same tree, parenting and transforms collapse and the asset does not assemble at all.
note: It carries a subject's claims, consents and pointers rather than a tree of scene objects, and its standards page lists scene graph rendering among the things it leaves alone.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: It places nothing in space, so it defines no handedness, axis order or transform composition.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: It carries no geometry and no scene. Its relation to a spatial fabric or an asset is a pointer and nothing more, and a pointer is required to carry a type and a target and nothing else.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A mesh encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a mesh, and the compression choice is where this usually breaks.
note: It defines no mesh encoding or compression; geometry stays in the files that pointers reference.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Device-specific texture compression is the common failure: the model arrives untextured and someone must re-export it.
note: It defines no image formats or texture compression; textures stay in referenced files.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Carrying materials without loss is what "renders in another system" means, and only two subjects reach this row natively today.
note: It carries no material definitions between renderers because it describes no surface appearance.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A clip that cannot be read leaves the object still, and an avatar that cannot move is not an avatar.
note: It stores no keyframes or clips; animation, like other heavy data, stays in referenced files.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The bone hierarchy is what makes a body move correctly elsewhere; without an agreed one, motion has nothing to bind to.
note: Searched Universal Manifest v0.4 Primer, Base, EXT-T1, EXT-T2, EXT-T3, EXT-OPT, Cookbook and document-set index for skeleton, bone, rig, humanoid, skin on 2026-10-20; the only hit is a consent key naming a hand skeleton. A body's bone hierarchy and binding stay in whatever file a pointer references.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Blend shapes carry facial detail, so losing them freezes a face rather than stopping the transfer.
note: It defines no shape deformation data; morph targets belong to the mesh files a pointer would reference.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A scene without agreed instancing still loads, it just costs far more memory and frames.
note: It describes no scene content, so repeating an object cheaply is not something it can express or needs to.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Layered references are a working convenience, and flattening on export is the fallback that keeps the asset moving.
note: Its composition is of facets inside one signed envelope, not layering or overriding parts of a scene from several sources.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A metre read as a centimetre makes the asset useless on arrival, and rescaling by hand is the fix the use case forbids.
note: It describes no scene content, so it has no real-world scale to agree on.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: An item that arrives with no readable terms cannot be lawfully worn, shown or sold, so the move fails at the rights boundary even when every byte arrives.
note: A preview, design-stage profile binds a signed record to the exact asset bytes and lists permitted-use verbs such as display, port, transform, train and commercial use. The grantor is the person depicted in the asset, not the rights holder, so this is consent travelling with the asset rather than a licence.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A signed record of who made an asset lets a receiver trust it; without one the asset still works but nobody can check its history.
note: Universal Manifest signs with Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON, bound to a key named by a decentralized identifier. The RP1 fabric it points at signs with a compact JSON Web Signature, RS256 and an X.509 chain. A verifier for one cannot verify the other, and the project's integration resolved that by refusing to merge them: the bridge is a pointer from the manifest to the fabric URL, never a re-signing. They answer different questions, who the person is and who published these bytes, and both are needed. The public specification states the profile; the framing of it as deliberately not a JSON Web Signature, and the bridge decision, are the project's own record.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/core/ | Fabric file entity document, web reader limit (observed, no public source states it)

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The portable description of the body is the artefact this use case moves; with no agreement the person arrives as nothing.
note: Universal Manifest points at an avatar and never describes one. Pointers exist precisely so that heavy files stay where they are, so format, rig, scale and wearables are somebody else's problem by declaration.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Agreed bone names are what let animation authored anywhere play on the arriving body.
note: Searched Universal Manifest v0.4 Primer, Base, EXT-T1, EXT-T2, EXT-T3, EXT-OPT, Cookbook and document-set index for skeleton, bone, rig, humanoid on 2026-10-20; the only hit is a consent key naming a hand skeleton. The envelope points at an avatar file and leaves bone naming and structure to it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The use case names expressions, and named shapes the destination does not know leave a blank face.
note: Searched Universal Manifest v0.4 Primer, Base, EXT-T1, EXT-T2, EXT-T3, EXT-OPT, Cookbook and document-set index for viseme, blend shape, morph, facial, expression on 2026-10-20; nothing defines named expressions or visemes. The envelope points at an avatar file and leaves expression data to it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Retargeting is the repair when skeletons differ, so its absence costs motion quality rather than the visit.
note: Searched Universal Manifest v0.4 Primer, Base, EXT-T1, EXT-T2, EXT-T3, EXT-OPT, Cookbook and document-set index for retarget, animation on 2026-10-20; no hit. The specification does not describe how animation authored for one body plays on another.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Equipped items are named in the use case, and attachment points that do not survive leave items on the floor or on the wrong bone.
note: Searched Universal Manifest v0.4 Primer, Base, EXT-T1, EXT-T2, EXT-T3, EXT-OPT, Cookbook and document-set index for wearable, garment, clothing, equipment, loadout, attachment point on 2026-10-20; the only hits are a device class for wearable sensors and an unrelated attachment of a pose value. Worn items and their attachment points are not defined.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Reduced forms matter for crowds and weak devices, and their absence costs frames, not presence.
note: Searched Universal Manifest v0.4 Primer, Base, EXT-T1, EXT-T2, EXT-T3, EXT-OPT, Cookbook and document-set index for LOD, level of detail on 2026-10-20; no hit. The specification defines no reduced avatar representations.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Without a way to bind an avatar to a verifiable identity, the person who arrives cannot be shown to be the person who left.
note: The binding is real but it is generic, and a working group should know which half is standardised. The specification defines a typed pointer array: every pointer must carry a type and a target, the pointers sit inside the bytes the signature covers, and an evaluator meeting a pointer type it does not recognise must record it and must not act on it. It names no avatar pointer. The avatar meaning comes from usage: the published cookbook's complete manifest, Example 22, carries an avatar as a generic mediaRef pointer whose target is an avatar file, and a third-party implementation defaults to the pointer name portableIdentity.avatar for the published XR fixtures. So a destination can check that this person really claims this avatar, and it learns nothing about what the avatar file contains.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Mass and velocity carried across make a moved object behave nearly the same; their absence changes the behaviour without stopping it.
note: It simulates nothing, and its standards page lists physics among the things it leaves alone.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Collision shapes travel separately from visible geometry, and losing them means objects pass through each other until the destination builds its own.
note: It has no contact tests or shapes, and its standards page lists physics among the things it leaves alone.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Hinges and sliders that do not survive turn an assembly into loose parts, which is a loss of behaviour rather than of the asset.
note: It links no bodies, and its standards page lists physics among the things it leaves alone.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Friction and restitution numbers mean different things to different solvers, so agreeing on them buys little and each world may keep its own feel.
note: It defines no surface response, and its standards page lists physics among the things it leaves alone.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Two engines producing the same trajectory would let one object be simulated in two places at once, and nothing does that today.
note: It runs no simulation, and its standards page lists physics among the things it leaves alone.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Cloth and hair are the visible part, so a moved avatar arrives stiff rather than absent.
note: It simulates nothing, and its standards page lists physics among the things it leaves alone.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Regions that fire events are part of how content behaves, and their loss makes the content inert rather than unreadable.
note: It has no volumes that fire events, and its standards page lists physics among the things it leaves alone.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Positioned sounds are authored into a scene, and losing them leaves a silent room.
note: It carries no audio and places no sound in a scene; media stays outside the handshake.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: How direction is turned into sound at the ears is the receiving system's method, like a rendering method.
note: It renders no sound, so it has no head-related or ambisonic model.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A space's acoustic description is authored with it, and without agreement the room sounds wrong rather than silent.
note: It describes no space and renders no sound, so room acoustics are outside it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The receiving runtime works this out from its own geometry, frame by frame.
note: It has no geometry or audio path, so sound blocking is outside it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A visitor can be given audio by other means, so disagreement costs quality and scale.
note: It delivers no media streams; they stay outside the handshake.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A visitor who cannot be heard is diminished but still present, and text remains a fallback.
note: It carries no live voice; at most it holds consent for audio-derived data.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A client or agent that cannot read the destination's state stream arrives blind, which ends both use cases on the spot.
note: It shares no live world state; it is evaluated once on arrival and nothing re-checks during a session.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Disagreement about who owns an arriving object shows up as rubber-banding and contested edits rather than as a failed arrival.
note: It decides no object truth in a running world; it records who a subject is and what they consented to.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Without agreement the destination sends everything or too little, which costs scale.
note: It sends no per-client world data, so interest management is outside it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Latency hiding is local repair work, so its absence is felt as lag.
note: It has no live simulation to predict or reconcile.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: With no shared wire protocol there is no session to join at all.
note: Explicitly not a host, a store or a transport. The envelope is fetched over whatever the deployment uses and the specification is careful to keep transport out: it notes that two devices may exchange manifests over a local link such as near-field, Bluetooth or a printed code and each verify the other without a server.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Live audio and video degrade or drop out while the visit continues.
note: It carries no live audio or video; media stays outside the handshake.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Joining a running world, authentication included, is the door: no agreement, no entry.
note: The base model still evaluates at a boundary: a document arrives, six stages run in order, a receipt is written, and nothing in the base re-checks anything while an interaction is running. A bilateral session model does exist but it is carried in the optional-features profile and marked preview. That matters because the gap has now been filled from the other side: TeleportXR, which lives entirely in the during-session layer, has shipped a message that invalidates an accepted avatar mid-session, and nothing on this side is specified to drive it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: This row is the portal itself, and the travel use case is nothing but the handoff.
note: The envelope is the state that crosses the boundary, and the specification supplies the general machinery: facets, claims, consents and pointers inside one signed document that a destination evaluates on arrival. What crossed in practice, pose, session, equipment, a continuity identifier and fifteen manifest facets between two separate world servers, together with the fail-closed gate that decided whether traversal was allowed at all, is the project's own working crossing and has no public source. What it did not carry was velocity, and it performed no scale or precision change.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/core/ | Open Spatial Lab design note, precision domain (observed composition failure, no public source states it)

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A roster that does not cross operators means you cannot see who is where, but you can still be there.
note: Presence falls inside what it gates: it defines a delegation scope for representing the subject's presence status and receipt events for presence and avatar disclosure, and the project says a facet can carry place membership. It carries no state of who is where and no presence protocol between operators. Searched Universal Manifest v0.4 Primer, Base, EXT-T1, EXT-T2, EXT-T3, EXT-OPT, Cookbook and document-set index and the project home and standards pages for presence, roster, who is where, online status, session membership, place membership on 2026-10-20; the hits are the presence-status scope, the disclosure receipt events, liveness attestation of human presence (a different matter) and the standards page's place membership, and none defines presence state or its exchange.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A destination name that does not resolve cannot be travelled to, so naming and resolution are the first agreement.
note: A manifest is fetched from an address, or resolved from a short identifier by a hosted resolver, and the manifest points onward at the things it describes. The resolver is a locator and nothing more: a third-party implementation records that although the resolver serves a one-minute HTTP cache header, consumers must enforce the manifest's own lifetime regardless of HTTP caching, so resolution and trust stay separate steps.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/ | Spatial fabric ecosystem map, typology catalog

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Worlds can be reached by a known address, so discovery adds reach rather than making it possible.
note: It is a handshake between parties that already meet, and its own text leaves even the discovery of status resolvers out of scope.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A shared clock keeps events in order; without one the ordering drifts and coarse clocks still hold the session together.
note: The specification defines issuedAt and expiresAt timestamps, a clock-skew tolerance of at most 60 seconds, and rejection of a manifest dated in the future. Freshness is judged against each evaluator's own clock; there is no shared time source or event-ordering model.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: With no shared base identifier the same person or agent is a stranger in every world they enter.
note: The signature block names its verification key by URI reference and the specification requires that reference to be present, recommending a decentralized identifier URL or an HTTPS URL. An embedded public key may travel beside it for offline verification, but the reference itself must still resolve. A third-party implementation states the reason plainly: accepting an inline key without checking it against the reference is exactly what would let an attacker re-sign a modified document with their own key.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Claims about age, membership or ownership are worthless if the receiving world cannot read them.
note: This is the subject's core and it is now published in full. Signature Profile A is the baseline normative profile: RFC 8785 canonical JSON with the signature member removed, signed with Ed25519, the value base64url without padding. The evaluator checklist is ordered and mandatory, and a manifest whose only signature uses an unsupported profile is rejected rather than accepted quietly. The context document is pinned by its own content hash, so the meaning of the terms cannot be swapped underneath a verifier.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A credential nobody can ask for or present is not a credential, and one subject reaches this row natively today.
note: The base model is still an evaluation of a presented document rather than an interactive request-and-present protocol, and the interactive parts, holder binding and presentation proof, live in a companion profile with several sections still marked preview. But the older reading of this row, that the three specifications it would present to all leave the slot empty and no plug is specified, is no longer true. One of the three now has a plug: the public TeleportXR repository accepts a manifest address in place of an avatar URL, resolves it, verifies Signature Profile A, and answers with a receipt. A live replay weakness found in the project's own reciprocal-control holder binding, and fixed locally by binding the full content hash, was never delivered upstream; that remains a project-local record.
sources: https://github.com/teleportxr/Teleport/blob/main/docs/protocol/signaling.rst | https://github.com/teleportxr/Teleport/blob/main/TeleportCore/export_include/TeleportCore/Manifest.h | https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/ext-t1/ | Upstream register, item B5 (this project's own label, no public source states it)

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A world that cannot read what an arriving person or agent is allowed to do must either refuse it or trust it blindly.
note: Permission is expressed as consent records inside the signed envelope, each naming the operations it allows, the purpose it allows them for, and a validity window; a separate pointer type declares delegated session authority for an agent. The evaluation rule is default-deny and it is normative: a facet with no consent entry governing it is recorded as consent-missing, and an evaluator must not process facet data when required consent is absent, expired or withdrawn. Every decision, allow or refuse, is recorded in a structured receipt.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Without selective disclosure the traveller over-shares, which is a harm rather than a stop.
note: Selective disclosure is a normative stage of the evaluation sequence rather than an add-on: the evaluator must extract only the facets, claims, pointers and device entries relevant to its processing context, and the specification calls this the bounded selective minimum disclosure profile. Beneath it sit encrypted facets, sealed with JSON Web Encryption inside the envelope, where a facet the evaluator cannot open must be acknowledged as present but unread rather than guessed at or treated as a failure. The stronger tracks, zero-knowledge proofs and unlinkable disclosure, are published as preview and should not be counted as shipping.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Relationships and standing that do not travel leave the person present but unknown.
note: Standing between parties is expressed, a relationship graph is not. The optional-features profile defines a typed trust weight and category trust, and a bilateral session model where two parties each evaluate the other and each keeps a receipt. There is no follower model, no portable contact list and no social graph of any kind.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The terms themselves must cross, and that row is a must; acting on them is the receiver's own behaviour, and no agreed mechanism exists yet.
note: Terms are acted on at the point of use, but the terms are consents rather than licences: an operation outside the granted scope, or a use outside the declared purpose, is refused and recorded, and an expired or withdrawn grant is treated as absent. There is no licence vocabulary and no enforcement of asset rights. The worked example of a denied cross-world link keeping a link local is the project's own integration and has no public source.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/core/ | RP1 entity document, delivery observation (observed, no public source states the CORS posture)

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Content pinned to the Earth must land in the same place in the other system, and a pose that cannot be read puts it somewhere else.
note: This row previously claimed a working geographic pose and that was too generous. The published specification lists a GeoPose primary pose value profile among its design-stage candidate profiles, marked preview and not yet on the wire, and states that the candidate members are absent from the published schema, context and fixtures until finalized. The published v0.4 context confirms it: none of its terms names a pose, a coordinate, a geographic frame or a spatial anchor. The spatial bookmarks pairing a fabric identifier with a pose exist in this project's own material and not in the specification.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/core/ | https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/ext-opt/ | https://universalmanifest.net/ns/v0.4 | Universal Manifest entity document, section 1

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A frame disagreement is measured in metres or kilometres, not in taste.
note: Through the optional GeoPose Primary Pose Value Profile (EXT-OPT O14, marked PREVIEW and design-stage, not yet in the schema or conformance fixtures), a subject whose main fact is position and orientation should carry its pose as an OGC GeoPose 1.0 payload in a geographically anchored frame, so the frame is agreed by delegation to OGC GeoPose. The profile does not convert between reference frames or resolve ambiguity in external frame definitions.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: An anchor made on one device never leaves it; the sharing case is the next row.
note: It fixes no content to a place on a device, and its standards page leaves spatial anchor coordinate systems to the spatial runtime.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Two people in two systems must see the same thing in the same spot, and today one subject reaches this row, through an extension.
note: Through the optional GeoPose Primary Pose Value Profile (EXT-OPT O14, marked PREVIEW and design-stage), a manifest whose subject is a real-world object, 3D asset or scene element can carry a signed GeoPose primary pose, inline as a geopose.primary claim or by a um:geoPosePrimary pointer bound by a SHA-256 digest, which fixes the content to a geographic place any device can read. Missing: anchor persistence and resolution, and device-relative (non-geographic) shared anchors, which are not defined. Searched Universal Manifest v0.4 Primer, Base, EXT-T1, EXT-T2, EXT-T3, EXT-OPT, Cookbook and document-set index for spatial anchor, persistent anchor, cloud anchor, anchor on 2026-10-20; apart from O14, every hit is a semantic, trust or transparency-log anchor. The project's standards page says a facet can carry spatial anchor data, but defines no structure for it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Recovering pose from imagery can fall back to satellite position and manual alignment, at worse accuracy.
note: It processes no camera imagery and recovers no pose.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: City-scale data is streamed by tile, and a tileset the receiving client cannot stream has to be converted before it is usable.
note: It streams no geospatial data; heavy data stays in referenced files.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A structured description of an interior makes placement and routing better; without one both are cruder, and nothing reaches this row today.
note: It describes no interior spaces; its spatial content is limited to carrying a pose value in a design-stage profile.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The visitor's app and the device runtime are two independent systems, and if they cannot start an immersive session the visit does not happen.
note: Its session is an exchange of manifests between two parties, not the starting, running and ending of an immersive session on a device.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A world that reads controllers differently is harder to use, and pointer and text paths remain.
note: It reads no handheld devices; it carries no input streams.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Hand tracking adds a way in, and its absence falls back to controllers.
note: It delivers no hand pose; it only defines a consent key for hand data.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Gaze is an aid with privacy limits, and everything works without it.
note: A preview profile defines consent keys that separate a raw gaze stream from region-of-interest results, each bound to a purpose and refused unless explicitly granted, which covers the privacy-constraint half of the definition. It does not define gaze direction as an input source or how it is delivered.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Touch feedback is felt when it is missing, and nothing stops.
note: It sends no touch feedback to a user.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A world that cannot ask what the arriving device can do will guess, and guessing wrong costs quality rather than entry.
note: The preview two-component devices schema in the optional-features profile lets a manifest declare sensors, supported OpenXR extensions, positioning tier and processing limits for the current session. It is self-declared unless a manufacturer attestation is present, and the base specification only reserves the devices member.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The language a world writes its rules in is its own business and never has to cross.
note: It defines no scripting language or runtime; it is a document format with an evaluation contract.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The use case says the asset must behave, so a door that will not open in the second system is the failure this row names.
note: It carries no interactivity or executable content with an asset; its output is a verdict and a receipt.

subject: Universal Manifest

subject: Universal Manifest

Each version has its own document set, its own context URL and its own conformance fixtures, v0.3 is named as the stable published reference and v0.4 as the production-candidate milestone, and the specification states outright that while the line is still 0.x a minor bump may include breaking changes in a new version folder. subject: VRM
interop_reason: Authored viewpoints are part of a scene, and losing them costs the arrival shot, not the scene.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: If the receiving system cannot rebuild the same tree, parenting and transforms collapse and the asset does not assemble at all.
note: A VRM model is a glTF node tree, and VRM adds the parts that matter for a character: fixed parentage between named humanoid bones and a model space rooted at the scene root. Missing: VRM states that glTF represents an entire scene while VRM represents one humanoid, so it defines no relationships between several objects in a world.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: Handedness and axis order come from glTF and VRM restates none of it. VRM does add the convention glTF lacks for characters: in the rest pose the model stands facing positive Z, symmetrical about X, arms out along X, and every node scale must be uniform and positive. Missing: no transform convention of its own beyond the rest pose.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: Defines its own file: binary glTF with a required VRMC_vrm extension carrying specVersion, humanoid and meta, saved with the .vrm suffix. The container is glTF's; what makes it a VRM is the required extension.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A mesh encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a mesh, and the compression choice is where this usually breaks.
note: Mesh encoding is glTF's and VRM specifies none of it. What VRM adds is two restrictions aimed at making models load the same everywhere: stored tangents may be left out and recalculated, and morph target tangents should be neither exported nor imported.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Device-specific texture compression is the common failure: the model arrives untextured and someone must re-export it.
note: Image encoding is glTF's. VRM adds one restriction and it is a narrow one: the model thumbnail must be square and must be a jpg or png supported by glTF's core, with extension formats forbidden. Missing: nothing is said about texture compression for the model's own textures.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Carrying materials without loss is what "renders in another system" means, and only two subjects reach this row natively today.
note: A VRM model keeps its glTF core material, so a plain physically based renderer will show something. subject: VRM
interop_reason: A clip that cannot be read leaves the object still, and an avatar that cannot move is not an avatar.
note: A VRM file carries no animation: the core says the glTF animations and cameras arrays are not used. Humanoid motion lives in a separate file defined by VRMC_vrm_animation 1.0, which reuses glTF's own keyframe machinery and adds the mapping to named bones, expressions and gaze.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The bone hierarchy is what makes a body move correctly elsewhere; without an agreed one, motion has nothing to bind to.
note: Binding and skinning are glTF's; the part VRM adds is the mapping from each named human bone to a glTF node, which is what makes the rig readable by a runtime that never saw the model. Bone transforms are constrained further: scale must be uniform and positive.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Blend shapes carry facial detail, so losing them freezes a face rather than stopping the transfer.
note: The shape deformation itself is glTF's morph targets, which VRM does not change. What VRM adds is naming: expressions bind groups of morph targets to an agreed name, and because glTF has no name for a morph target the specification recommends putting one in the mesh extras. Missing: VRM specifies no encoding of its own.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A scene without agreed instancing still loads, it just costs far more memory and frames.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Layered references are a working convenience, and flattening on export is the fallback that keeps the asset moving.
note: A VRM file is one self-contained humanoid. There is no referencing another file, no layering and no override, which is the structural reason a wearable cannot be shipped separately from the avatar it is worn on.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Without selective disclosure the traveller over-shares, which is a harm rather than a stop.

subject: VRM

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Content pinned to the Earth must land in the same place in the other system, and a pose that cannot be read puts it somewhere else.
note: An avatar file measures its parts in a model space relative to its own scene root and places the avatar nowhere on the Earth. Position and orientation against the Earth belong to the world that hosts the avatar, not to a humanoid avatar format.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A frame disagreement is measured in metres or kilometres, not in taste.
note: VRM fixes one local frame for the avatar: a model space measured from the root of the glTF scene, in metres, with the rest pose facing positive Z. Missing: no way to declare or name a coordinate reference system, and nothing relates the frame to a shared or geographic one.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Two people in two systems must see the same thing in the same spot, and today one subject reaches this row, through an extension.
note: An avatar file is not fixed to a place and has no anchor, so fixing content to a location across devices and sessions is not what a humanoid avatar format is for.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: City-scale data is streamed by tile, and a tileset the receiving client cannot stream has to be converted before it is usable.
note: VRM carries one humanoid for one avatar, so streaming large geospatial 3D data by tile is not something it does or could be asked to do.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The visitor's app and the device runtime are two independent systems, and if they cannot start an immersive session the visit does not happen.
note: Starting, running and ending an immersive session on a device is a runtime matter; VRM describes one avatar file and has no session.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The language a world writes its rules in is its own business and never has to cross.
note: The VRM specification says VRM represents a humanoid for a VR avatar, where glTF represents an entire scene. No language, no runtime, no executable content of any kind.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The use case says the asset must behave, so a door that will not open in the second system is the failure this row names.
note: Searched the 17 English specification documents of vrm-c/vrm-specification at commit 94e82dd (core extension, expressions, humanoid, first person, look-at, meta, T-pose, spring bone and its collider and limit extensions, node constraint, MToon, emissive multiplier, VRM animation) for script, event, trigger, interactive, executable, state machine and behaviour on 2026-10-19; found no scripting, event or trigger construct, and the word behaviour appears only for how a solver or reader should act. subject: VRM
interop_reason: An agent with no agreed way to perceive and act in a world it did not come from cannot join it at all.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The use case names inventory, and items that cannot be read at the destination do not travel with the person.
note: VRM is the avatar file that may travel, not the record of items a user holds or the rules for whether they travel; that record belongs to the platform that keeps it.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The use case names preferences, and for a person who depends on comfort and accessibility settings, arriving without them ends the visit.
note: Settings and accessibility choices that follow a user are held by a platform or account; a VRM file describes the avatar and carries no user settings.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A runnable experience moves between hosts far less often than an asset does, and repackaging is the fallback.
note: VRM packages one avatar as a single .glb file with a .vrm suffix, which is an asset container and not a runnable experience; packaging an experience belongs to a different layer.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Assets reach clients over ordinary web delivery, so agreement here buys scale and cost rather than possibility.
note: Getting assets to clients at scale is a hosting matter; VRM defines the avatar file and says nothing about how it is distributed.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A reader that cannot tell which version it holds, or what to do with the parts it does not know, breaks on the first update, which is the "no hand fixes" test again.
note: Each extension carries its own version string, so a reader can tell what it is holding. Missing: no compatibility rule. VRM 0.x is a different extension key holding a different shape of data, so a 1.0 reader cannot read a 0.x file and the older line is now deprecated rather than bridged.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Every other must row is a claim until a shared test says it holds, which is exactly what the meeting asked for.

subject: VRM
capability: World generation from a prompt or an image

note: VRM is a glTF extension set for one humanoid avatar at rest, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A world continued by a model still reaches a viewer, but only as what the model chooses to show, so the receiver cannot keep it or run it again.
note: VRM is a glTF extension set for one humanoid avatar at rest, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: How a system turns photographs into a model is its own method, and what leaves is an ordinary asset the container and geometry rows already carry.
note: VRM is a glTF extension set for one humanoid avatar at rest, and turning a set of ordinary photographs into a textured three-dimensional model is not among its jobs.

subject: VRM
